ApprovePolicyRequest.description:
Approve REUSE of the decision this case already made.

Separate from resolving the case, deliberately: a one-time resolution is
never auto-promoted into a reusable rule. The scope is the case's own
vendor and effect; only the validity window is chosen here.
ApprovePolicyRequest.title: ApprovePolicyRequest

ResolutionOptionOut.description:
One rate a human may choose when resolving a contract-term conflict.

Derived from the case's own `evidence_refs`, never supplied by the caller:
the options are exactly the candidate terms the detector cited, so a client
cannot introduce a rate nobody detected.
ResolutionOptionOut.title: ResolutionOptionOut

ResolveCaseRequest.description:
Two accepted shapes for one command.

The original shape states the rate directly: `decision` of
approve/edit/reject plus `commission_bps`. Scripts and the verify suites
use it and it is unchanged.

The reviewer-facing shape names the option instead:
`decision: "ACCEPT_OPTION" | "REJECT"` with `option_id`, and binds the
decision to what the reviewer actually saw via `evidence_hash` and
`expected_version`. The rate then comes from the case's own evidence, so
the client never supplies the number that decides money.
ResolveCaseRequest.title: ResolveCaseRequest

get.description:
The C05 business configuration: how this festival charges and pays.

The finance posting config carries the versioned, stored part (timezone,
the 9 AM / 10 AM times, the forecast horizon, the tax configuration). The
rest -- the default terms a vendor falls back to and the payout controls --
lives in the domain package as the constants the engines actually apply, so
it is read from there rather than restated. If a value here disagreed with
what settlement and release use, this endpoint would be the thing that is
wrong.

`currency` is C01's fixed USD for v1. `draft_notice` carries the config's
own label, so nobody reads these as approved business facts.

get.description:
The festival this deployment operates.

A registered festival wins: registering one is the explicit statement of
which festival this is, and a dev or test database can hold dozens of
derived ids from fixtures. With exactly one registered we return it; with
several, this is ambiguous and the caller has to name one, so we say so
rather than guessing. With none registered we fall back to the derived
record carrying the most business dates, so a fresh database still answers.

Every festival that can be resolved, by id. `next_cursor` is always
null: a festival is a workspace-level record (there are a handful, not a
stream of them), so the envelope keeps the shape every other list here
uses without pretending to page.

Cursor paging, same offset-cursor convention as `GET /journal`: the
cursor is an opaque decimal offset over a stable (name, id) order, and
`next_cursor` is null on the last page. `festival_id` is optional so a
single vendor-name lookup table can be loaded without one.

Process is up. No external dependency check -- this must stay cheap
and always answer even if the database is unreachable, so orchestrators
can distinguish 'process is wedged' from 'dependency is down'.
Process is up AND can reach Postgres.
